prompt: A router's average offered load rises from 80% to 90% of link capacity. Traffic remains bursty. Why can queueing delay grow much more sharply than the traffic rate?

options.text: Queueing delay must always change in direct proportion to average load
options.explanation: Average load does not capture the nonlinear effect of having little spare capacity to drain bursts.

options.text: Less spare service capacity remains to clear temporary backlogs
options.explanation: Correct. Bursts take longer to drain near capacity; the exact delay depends on arrival patterns, service and scheduling.

options.text: A link below 100% load cannot have queues
options.explanation: Bursts can exceed service capacity temporarily even when average offered load is below capacity.

options.text: At 90% load every real router has an infinite mean delay
options.explanation: That does not follow. Even the stated stable M/M/1 model has a finite mean below full load, and real buffers are finite.

workedExample: Average spare capacity is what drains a backlog after a burst. As that margin shrinks, a small traffic increase can leave packets waiting much longer. The M/M/1 example illustrates this effect under its random-arrival and random-service assumptions; use measurements and an appropriate model for actual delay.
